title: Joint Pain and Swelling Assessment
summary: A clinician-facing prompt for assessing joint pain, distinguishing monoarticular from polyarticular presentations, identifying septic joint and other urgent causes.

sections.title: Assessment priorities
sections.intro: Use this guide as a prompt. It does not replace clinical judgement, urgent investigation or escalation.

items.title: Must confirm or exclude
mustConfirmOrExclude: Septic arthritis (fever, acute joint swelling, inability to weight-bear, warmth, severe pain).
Gout (acute monoarticular, severe pain, podagra common, urate history).
Crystal arthropathy or pseudogout (acute swelling, crystals on microscopy).
Fracture or ligamentous injury (trauma history, severe pain, swelling, inability to function).
Rheumatoid arthritis or seronegative spondyloarthropathy (polyarticular, morning stiffness, symmetric).
Inflammatory bowel disease with arthropathy or reactive arthritis (extraarticular features).
Malignancy (weight loss, systemic illness, polyarticular).
items.importantLimitation: Septic joint can be missed with mild fever. Monoarticular presentation with fever requires joint aspiration to exclude infection.

items.title: Onset and characteristics
mustConfirmOrExclude: Onset: sudden vs. gradual; triggered by specific event or spontaneous.
Duration: hours, days, weeks.
Course: acute onset vs. gradual progression over weeks/months.
Pain character: sharp, aching, throbbing or inflammatory.
Swelling: immediately vs. delayed; visible vs. palpable.

items.title: Joint involvement pattern
mustConfirmOrExclude: Number of affected joints: single vs. multiple.
Pattern if polyarticular: symmetric vs. asymmetric; small vs. large joints.
Morning stiffness: present, duration (inflammatory suggests >1hr).
Joint history: previous episodes in same joint (recurrent gout).

items.title: Red-flag features
mustConfirmOrExclude: Fever with acute joint swelling (septic arthritis).
Trauma or fall preceding pain (fracture, ligament injury).
Recent injection or procedure (post-injection septic joint).
IV drug use (endocarditis + septic joint).
Immunosuppression or prosthetic joint (infection risk).
Severe systemic illness with joint pain (sepsis, malignancy).
Rash with joint pain (viral, SLE, rheumatic fever).

items.title: Features suggesting inflammatory arthritis
mustConfirmOrExclude: Morning stiffness >1 hour (rheumatoid arthritis).
Polyarticular symmetric involvement (RA typical).
Systemic symptoms: fatigue, malaise, weight loss.
Family history of autoimmune disease.
Preceding URI or GI symptoms (reactive arthritis).
Eye involvement, uveitis or oral ulcers.

items.title: Septic arthritis
urgentFeatures: Fever with acute joint swelling and severe pain.
Inability to weight-bear or move joint passively.
Warmth and erythema over joint.
Often monoarticular; large joints (knee, hip) common.
Risk factors: immunosuppression, prosthetic joint, IV drug use.
implications: Emergency hospital assessment; joint aspiration and culture mandatory.

items.title: Gout or crystal arthropathy
urgentFeatures: Acute severe monoarticular pain, often at night.
Podagra (big toe) classic but any joint can be affected.
Swelling appears rapidly.
History of gout or urate elevation.
Triggers: purine-rich food, alcohol, diuretics.
implications: NSAID or colchicine for acute pain; uric acid management long-term.

items.title: Fracture or significant ligament injury
urgentFeatures: Trauma preceding pain; often severe pain with swelling.
Inability to weight-bear or function.
Deformity, crepitus or instability on examination.
Swelling appears immediately or rapidly.
implications: X-ray or advanced imaging; orthopedic assessment if significant.

items.title: Polyarticular inflammatory arthritis
urgentFeatures: Multiple joints affected; often symmetric.
Morning stiffness >1 hour.
Systemic symptoms (fatigue, fever, weight loss).
Acute rheumatoid arthritis, SLE or viral arthritis.
implications: Bloods (CRP, ESR, RF, anti-CCP, ANA); rheumatology referral.

items.title: Reactive arthritis
urgentFeatures: Polyarticular arthritis following URI or GI infection.
Often with urethritis or conjunctivitis (Reiter triad).
Non-erosive; self-limited.
implications: NSAIDs; resolves with management of preceding infection.

items.title: Joint examination
howToTest: Inspect: swelling, erythema, deformity, skin changes.
Palpate: warmth, fluctuance, tenderness (joint line vs. periarticular).
Range of motion: active and passive; pain with movement.
Stability tests: Lachman, ACL, collateral (knee); Sulcus sign (shoulder).
normal: No swelling, no warmth, full pain-free range of motion, stable.
abnormal: Swelling, warmth or erythema, restricted range, pain with passive movement, effusion, instability.
implications: Warmth + swelling + fever → septic joint. Acute swelling + pain without warmth → gout or trauma. Polyarticular + morning stiffness → inflammatory.

items.title: Systemic assessment
howToTest: Look for rash, nodules, or other systemic features.
Assess other joints for polyarticular pattern.
Evaluate functional status and weight-bearing ability.
normal: Afebrile or low-grade fever only; no systemic features; other joints normal.
abnormal: Fever >38.5°C, rash, systemic illness, polyarticular involvement.
implications: Fever + monoarticular swelling = septic until proven otherwise.

items.title: Acute gout attack
commonFindings: Sudden severe pain in big toe or foot (podagra).
Often triggered by alcohol, purine-rich food or diuretics.
implications: NSAIDs or colchicine acutely; long-term urate lowering.

items.title: Osteoarthritis
implications: Analgesics, physiotherapy; joint imaging for severity.

items.title: Viral arthritis
commonFindings: Follows viral illness; associated URI symptoms.

items.title: Rheumatoid arthritis (early)
implications: CRP, ESR, RF, anti-CCP; rheumatology referral for DMARD therapy.

items.title: Investigation approach
mustConfirmOrExclude: Joint aspiration with culture: essential if fever + acute monoarticular swelling (septic arthritis risk).
X-rays: for fracture, osteoarthritis or structural damage assessment.
Blood tests (CRP, ESR, RF, anti-CCP, ANA): if polyarticular or inflammatory features.
Uric acid level: if gout suspected.

items.title: Community management when
mustConfirmOrExclude: No fever or low-grade fever only.
No trauma history or features of fracture.
Likely gout, osteoarthritis or viral arthritis.
Able to function with simple analgesia.

items.title: Urgent hospital assessment
urgentFeatures: Fever with acute monoarticular swelling (septic arthritis until proven).
Severe pain with inability to weight-bear or move joint.
Trauma with suspected fracture or severe ligament injury.
Prosthetic joint with fever or swelling.
Polyarticular with systemic illness and high inflammatory markers.
implications: Same-day hospital assessment or ED referral required.

items.title: Joint pain and swelling
safetyNetting: Call 999 or go to ED immediately for: fever with acute joint swelling and severe pain; inability to move or weight-bear; signs of shock; or trauma with severe pain and deformity.

Contact your GP or go to ED same-day for: fever with joint swelling (exclude septic arthritis); severe acute joint pain; rapid swelling after trauma; polyarticular pain with systemic illness; or joint swelling not improving after 1 week.
Speak to your GP if: recurrent joint pain episodes; joint pain with morning stiffness; pain improving with NSAIDs but recurring; or you want investigation of chronic arthritis.
